title: Conditional Logic and Truth Tables
objectives: Build truth tables for compound propositions built from NOT, AND, OR and implication
State the one row in which a conditional $P \rightarrow Q$ is false, and why every other row is true
Verify the equivalences $P \rightarrow Q \equiv \neg P \vee Q$ and both De Morgan laws row by row
Distinguish the contrapositive from the converse and inverse using truth-table columns, and count satisfying assignments of a compound rule
motivation: Risk rules, alert conditions and code guards are compound logic: 'alert if the limit is breached OR the price is stale AND the order is large'. Whether such a rule fires is a truth-table question, and the same table proves when two written-down rules are secretly the same rule. Conditional logic also underwrites the deduction lesson: modus ponens is valid precisely because its truth table has no false rows.

blocks.md: A **proposition** is a sentence that is definitively true or false, and compound propositions are built with five connectives: negation $\neg P$, conjunction $P \wedge Q$ (both), inclusive disjunction $P \vee Q$ (at least one), implication $P \rightarrow Q$ (if-then), and biconditional $P \leftrightarrow Q$ (same value). A truth table is the contract: it lists every assignment of truth values and the resulting value. With $k$ distinct variables there are $2^k$ rows, so three variables mean eight rows, which is why tests love asking for the row count. AND and OR behave as expected; the connective that needs care is the implication.

blocks.caption: The conditional: false in exactly one row, true antecedent, false consequent.

blocks.md: $P \rightarrow Q$ is **false only when P is true and Q is false**; every other row is true. The surprising rows are the bottom two: with a false antecedent, the conditional says nothing that can fail, so it counts as true, 'if the market is closed, all orders queue' is a true promise on any day the market is open, precisely because the condition never bites. This is called vacuous truth, and it is what makes contrapositive reasoning sound.

blocks.md:
Each equivalence is checked by comparing columns across all four rows, do one by hand and the pattern sticks. De Morgan's laws are the workhorses: 'not (stale **and** large)' is 'not stale **or** not large', and negating an OR splits it into an AND of negations. A common slip is pushing negation inside without flipping the connective; $
eg(P \wedge Q) \equiv 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q$ is *false*, take P true and Q false: the left side is $
eg F = T$ while the right side is $F \wedge T = F$. One disagreeing row is enough. The lesson: never trust negation-pushing; verify with rows.

blocks.title: Worked: proving P ↔ Q equals (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P)
items: Row P=T, Q=T: $P \rightarrow Q$ is T and $Q \rightarrow P$ is T, so the conjunction is T; $P \leftrightarrow Q$ is T. Match.
Row P=T, Q=F: $P \rightarrow Q$ is F, so the conjunction is F; $P \leftrightarrow Q$ is F. Match.
Row P=F, Q=T: $P \rightarrow Q$ is T but $Q \rightarrow P$ is F, so the conjunction is F; $P \leftrightarrow Q$ is F. Match.
Row P=F, Q=F: both conditionals are T, so the conjunction is T; $P \leftrightarrow Q$ is T. Match.
All four rows agree: the biconditional is exactly 'both directions hold', which is why it reads 'if and only if'.

eg Q ightarrow 
eg P$ matches in all four rows.

blocks.text: Where this bites in real systems

blocks.md: Guards in code are compound propositions evaluated row by row at runtime. De Morgan's laws justify the rewrite `!(a && b)` to `!a || !b` and back, and short-circuit evaluation follows the truth table: in `p or expensive_check()`, if `p` is true the disjunction is already true and the second operand is never evaluated, a correctness-preserving optimisation only because OR is determined by its first true operand. Counting satisfying assignments is the table's other job: a rule true in 5 of 8 configurations fires for 5 flag combinations, the kind of 'how many cases make this true' question reasoning tests ask in numeric form. Note also that logical OR is **inclusive**: 'limit breached or stale price' fires if both hold; exclusive XOR fires only when exactly one does, and is true in just 2 of the 4 rows.

blocks.title: English 'or' is often exclusive; logic OR is not
blocks.md: 'You may have the coupon or the discount' usually means not both. In logic and in code, $P \vee Q$ is true when both hold. When a risk rule says 'OR', assume inclusive unless it says 'but not both', misreading this silently widens alert coverage.

blocks.title: Companion practice: the Mental Math page
blocks.md: Row counting under time pressure is a speed skill like any other: the platform's Mental Math page builds the timed-drill habit, and a few of its rapid-fire items double as boolean warm-ups. The goal is that building an 8-row table costs you seconds, not minutes.

guidedExercise.prompt:
Build the full truth tables for $
eg(P \wedge Q)$ and for $
eg P \vee 
eg Q$, row by row, confirm the two final columns are identical, and state the law this demonstrates. Then point at the single row that refutes the tempting (but wrong) claim $
eg(P \wedge Q) \equiv 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q$.
hints: Four rows: TT, TF, FT, FF. Evaluate the inner $P \wedge Q$ first, then negate.
For the wrong claim, look for a row where the two sides disagree.
De Morgan: negation flips AND to OR.
guidedExercise.solution:
Rows: P=T,Q=T: $P \wedge Q = T$ so $
eg(P \wedge Q) = F$; and $
eg P \vee 
eg Q = F \vee F = F$. P=T,Q=F: inner F, left side T; $
eg P \vee 
eg Q = F \vee T = T$. P=F,Q=T: T; $T \vee F = T$. P=F,Q=F: inner F, left side T; $T \vee T = T$. Columns identical: **De Morgan's first law**. The refutation row for the wrong claim is P=T, Q=F: there $
eg(P \wedge Q)$ is T but $
eg P \wedge 
eg Q = F \wedge T = F$ - one disagreeing row kills the equivalence.

independentExercise.prompt: A risk system alerts when: limit breached $L$, OR price stale $S$ AND order large $M$ - that is, alert $= L \vee (S \wedge M)$. (a) With $L = F$, $S = T$, $M = T$, does the alert fire? (b) Of the 8 combinations of $(L, S, M)$, how many fire the alert? (c) With the flags as in (a), list which single-flag flips would silence the alert.
hints: Evaluate the AND first, then the OR.
Count: rows with $L = T$ all fire; what does $L = F$ leave?
The alert currently fires because of the (S AND M) branch, since L is false.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $S \wedge M = T \wedge T = T$, and $F \vee T = T$ - **the alert fires**, via the AND branch. (b) Rows with $L = T$: 4 combinations (the OR is satisfied regardless). Rows with $L = F$: only $S = T, M = T$ fires, 1 more. Total $4 + 1 = \textbf{5}$ of 8. (c) The firing came only from $S \wedge M$ (as $L = F$), so flipping $S$ to F **or** $M$ to F silences it; flipping $L$ to T would fire it even harder. Two single flips work.

commonMistakes: Treating $P \rightarrow Q$ as false whenever P is false: the conditional is true on both false-P rows (vacuous truth).

Pushing negation through without flipping the connective: $
eg(P \wedge Q)$ is $
eg P \vee 
eg Q$, not $
eg P \wedge 
eg Q$.
Confusing the contrapositive with the converse or the inverse, compare the columns: only the contrapositive matches the original in all rows.
Reading OR as exclusive in logic rules; $P \vee Q$ is true when both hold, and XOR is a different, stricter connective.
Building a 4-row table for a 3-variable formula: $k$ variables need $2^k$ rows, so 3 variables mean 8.
realWorldApplication: Configuration validation and alert routing in production systems are truth tables in disguise: every combination of feature flags must be checked, and `!(a && b)` versus `!a || !b` rewrites are De Morgan's laws keeping hot-path guards correct.
quantFinanceApplication: Pre-trade risk checks are compound conditionals, breach OR (stale AND large), and a rule that fires in 5 of 8 flag states behaves very differently from one firing in 3: counting satisfying assignments from the truth table is how such rules are audited before they guard real money.
summary: A formula with $k$ variables has $2^k$ truth-table rows; build them systematically (TT, TF, FT, FF) and never skip one.
$P \rightarrow Q$ is false in exactly one row. P true, Q false, and is equivalent to $\neg P \vee Q$.
De Morgan: negating an AND gives an OR of negations, and vice versa; negation always flips the connective.
Only the contrapositive $\neg Q \rightarrow \neg P$ is equivalent to $P \rightarrow Q$; converse and inverse differ in the T,F row.
OR in logic is inclusive; short-circuit evaluation and satisfying-assignment counts are the runtime consequences of the table.

quiz.prompt: Under exactly which condition is the proposition $P \rightarrow Q$ false?
options: P is false and Q is false
P is true and Q is false
P is false and Q is true
P and Q have the same truth value
quiz.explanation: The conditional fails only when a true antecedent is followed by a false consequent. With P false the implication is vacuously true on both rows.

quiz.prompt: How many rows does the full truth table of a formula with three distinct variables (say $P, Q, R$) have?
quiz.explanation: $2^3 = 8$ rows, every combination of three truth values. In general $2^k$ rows for $k$ variables.

quiz.prompt: Select every equivalence that is CORRECT.
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is implication-as-disjunction and option 3 is the definition of the biconditional, both hold in all rows. Options 2 and 4 each forget to flip the connective under negation: De Morgan demands OR after negating AND, and AND after negating OR.

quiz.prompt: Which formula is logically EQUIVALENT to $P \rightarrow Q$?
quiz.explanation: Only the contrapositive matches the original column in all four rows. Converse and inverse are true in the row P=T, Q=F where the original is false; the negation differs in three rows.

quiz.prompt: For how many of the four rows of $(P, Q)$ is the exclusive OR, $P \oplus Q$ (true when exactly one of P, Q is true), true?
quiz.explanation: XOR is true for (T,F) and (F,T), exactly one holds, and false for (T,T) and (F,F). Two of four rows.

quiz.prompt: In Python, the guard `if p or expensive_check():` skips evaluating `expensive_check()` in which case?
options: Only when expensive_check() would return True
quiz.explanation: Short-circuit OR: once the left operand is true the disjunction is already true, so the right operand is never evaluated. This matches the truth table, the (T, anything) rows are true regardless of Q.

flashcards.back: Only when P is true and Q is false. Both rows with P false are (vacuously) true. Equivalent to $\neg P \vee Q$.

flashcards.back: False, the single row where an implication is false. Python expresses P -> Q exactly as (not p) or q.
